# Assessment of owl limpet (*Lottia gigantea*) populations at sites within Crystal Cove State Marine Conservation Area

```{r load packages, include = FALSE}
install.packages("tidyverse")
library(tidyverse)
library(readxl)
```

## Project Summary:

*Once you have completed this entire assignment, come back and write a project summary here that covers the aims, research questions, and basic methods of this study.*

The aims of this project is to identify how several limpet variables relate to each other and how these variables differ by site and year. We wanted to find how limpet size and density differs between sample sites and years, and how limpet mass and territory size relate to each other.

To gather data, limpets and territory sizes were measured from Corona del Mar (2022), Treasure Cove (2023 and 2025), Shaws Cove (2024), and Heisler Park (2024). Limpets within a transect were counted, their shell length was measured in millimeters, and their territory size was measured using standardized nets.

Data analysis regarding population density, shell length, and territory size was conducted. Population density per square meter for each site and transect was calculated alongside various summary statistics to compare densities between sites. To see if groups were significantly different in length, t-tests were conducted on the two years of Treasure Cove data, and between observations from Heisler Park and Shaws Cove. Continuing with shell length data, tests of assumptions were applied before comparing Treasure Cove and Corona del Mar data via t-test to find significant differences in populations. Territory area and limpet mass were calculated from collected data and Fenberg's equation relating mass and shell length. The relationship between mass and territory area was then investigated and compared between sites. Assumptions of tests of linear regression were applied to this data, both variables were log-transformed, and a linear model was created to highlight the relationship via a best fit regression line. A logarithmic linear model was created for Fenberg's data to compare.

You have been given data from several locations and survey years:

- 2022: Corona del Mar (CDM) - size data only, taken haphazardly

- 2023: Treasure Cove (TC) - size data in 5-m transects, territories

- 2024: Heisler Park and Shaws Cove - size data in variable length transects, territories

- 2025: Treasure Cove (TC) - size data in 5-m transects, territories

#### 2.1. How many limpets did we measure at each site in each year for sizes?

Use nrow(), group_by() and count() to tally the limpet observations at each transect. We used the same transect numbers at Shaws and Heisler, so group_by() site as well.

```{r}
No_CDM_Sizes

No_CDM_Sizes |> nrow()  #just counting number of rows total, since dataframe doesn't have corona del mar --> 1767 total


## How many did we measure at each site? 
No_CDM_Sizes |> count(site)  #counting number of observations at each site, adds up to 1767 so yippee

No_CDM_Sizes |> group_by(site) |> group_by(transect_num) |> count() #grouping by site since shaws and heisler use same numbers, then grouping by transect number, then counting observations in each transect number
```

#### 2.2 What was the limpet density (i.e., limpets per square meter) for each transect?

Make a new dataframe out of the `No_CDM_Sizes` that has a column called *density,* that calculates the limpets per square meter for each transect. Remember that the transect included 1 meter on either side of the tape (total of 2 meters wide). Make sure to maintain the separation in year for the two Treasure Cove surveys using the `group_by()` function.

```{r}
#adding density column

Limpet_Density <- No_CDM_Sizes |> 
  group_by(year, site, transect_num, transect_length_m) |> #grouping by all the     variables i'll need, did NOT work without transect_num
  count() |>    #counting observations
  mutate(density = (n / (transect_length_m * 2))) #added a bunch of () just in case
 
#area = transect length * 2  because each transect is basically a rectangle, just with different lengths

view(Limpet_Density)      #lookin

```

Do you see any patterns just from examining this table of values?

- From this table, Treasure cove 2025 seems to have the lowest density while Shaws Cove 2024 has the highest. Transect length seems to not have anything to do with density- surprising since I assumed that longer transects would naturally result in higher densities. Density seems to be primarily dependent on site, and to a lesser extent, year.

#### 2.3. Calculating mean and standard error of population density

What was the mean limpets per square meter across all sites? And the standard deviation? And standard error?

```{r}

mean(Limpet_Density$density)                            #mean of all densities
sd(Limpet_Density$density)                              #std of all densities 
sd(Limpet_Density$density)/sqrt(sum(Limpet_Density$n))  #standard error

```

Now create a summary table in which you calculate separate mean and standard deviation for each site and year (Shaws vs. Heisler vs. Treasure Cove)? What was the standard error? Round the mean and standard error to one decimal place. (look up the `round()` function!)

```{r}
# use summarize() to calculate the mean and standard error (sd/sqrt(n)) for the two locations
LimpetPopSummary <- Limpet_Density |> group_by(year,site) |>  #grouping by site and year
  summarize(mean_d = round(mean(density), 1), #SUMMARIZE!!! mean, 1 decimal place
            std_d = round(sd(density), 1),    #standard deviation, 1 decimal place
            sample_size = n(),                #sample sizes, counted after being grouped
            se_d = round(std_d/(sqrt(sample_size)), 1) #standard eror 
  )
  
# Display your summary nicely using kable(). 
knitr::kable(LimpetPopSummary)

```

**Based on these plots, does your data meet assumptions for a t-test?**

T-Test assumptions (for a Student's T-test)

- Are the data continuous (i.e., not categorical/discrete)?

- Have the sample data been randomly sampled from a population?

- Is there homogeneity of variance (i.e., the variability of the data in each group is similar)?

- Is the distribution of the model residuals approximately normal?

#### 2.6. Does average number of owl limpets per square meter differ significantly between Heisler Park and Shaws Cove?

Filter the data to only include those sites before putting it into the `t.test()` function. These are a good comparison because they were measured in the same year with the same survey methods.

```{r t-test}
# run a t-test on your count data from each site (Limpet_Density)
ShawsHeislerDensity <- Limpet_Density |> filter(site == "Heisler Park" | site == "Shaws Cove" )  #filtering dataset to only include obersvations from Heisler OR Shaws


t.test( density ~ site, data = ShawsHeislerDensity) #runnin t test, dependent = density, site = independent, data = datasite to look into

```

Explain the results of this t-test. Are you surprised by this result, given the figure you made above? Why do you think the results are what they are?

- The results of this test show that the means of each group were different, but not in a statistically significant way because of the large p-value. The 95% confidence interval expresses what values the mean will fall between when the sample is repeated multiple times. The confidence interval from this t-test isn't that great and doesn't make sense for the data we're looking at, we can't get a negative limpet density value. These results are not surprising, the previous boxplot shows the averages of these two groups close together (about only 2 limpets apart). Each group's median line also overlaps with the others IQR range and their standard errors overlap within the barplot as well- all pointing towards that these two groups are not significantly different. These results might be due to similar conditions at both sites and the fact that these observations were taken in the same year.

#### 3.2. Is there a [statistically significant]{.underline} difference in [mean]{.underline} size between limpets measured at Treasure Cove (a relatively low-impact site) compared to CDM (a high impact site)?

We have a much larger sample size for shell lengths than we did for density, so we can apply our tests of assumptions more rigorously and demonstrate our various tests.

##### 3.2.1 [Determine whether a parametric or non-parametric test is appropriate.]{.underline}

T-Test assumptions (for a Student's T-test)

- Are the data continuous (i.e., not categorical/discrete)? **YES**

- Have the sample data been randomly sampled from a population? **(Yes)**

- Is there homogeneity of variance (i.e., the variability of the data in each group is similar)? **NO**

```{r}
## Test for Homogeneity of Variance with an F-Test

# create the appropriate filter to include only Treasure Cove and CDM data
CDM_TC_Sizes <- SizeData_2022_2025 |> filter( site == "Treasure Cove" | site == "Corona del Mar")    #filtering for only observaitons from Treasure Cove or Corona del Mar 

  
# set the linear model for testing the assumptions
model <- lm(shell_length_mm ~ site, data = CDM_TC_Sizes)   #setting up model, shell_length_mm = response, site = predictor, data = where to look 

# Examine plot of Residuals vs. Fitted values
plot(model, which = 1)        #plotting model, 1st plot 

# F-test for homogeneity of variance - if p-value < 0.05 then variances are different. 
var.test(shell_length_mm ~ site, data = CDM_TC_Sizes)   #testing with formula, shell_length is a function of site, data = where to look 

# NOTE: if your sample fails this test, have no fear! Welch's t-test (the default that R uses) is okay to use with unequal variances. 

```

- Is the distribution of the model residuals approximately normal?

```{r}
## Test for normality

# examine a QQ-plot
plot(model, which = 2)   #calling up model from before, 2nd plot 

# conduct a Shapiro-Wilk test on the residuals
shapiro.test(model$residuals)  #p value < 0.05 so model residuals are different from normal, but big sample size so we can't take it seriously 
```

Why will we not pay attention to this Shapiro-Wilk test result? Because the sample size is very large and Shapiro-Wilk is overly sensitive (gives false positives) at large sample sizes.

##### 3.2.2 [Conduct the test]{.underline}

```{r t-test or Wilcox}
# calculate the t-test results
t.test( shell_length_mm ~ site, data = CDM_TC_Sizes)  #t test!! shell length = response, site = predictor 

```

#### [3.4 - Interpret and explain the results of your test]{.underline}

Are we pretty confident that these samples were drawn from different populations? Why is the standard error so small?

- We can be pretty confident that these samples were drawn from different populations because of the very small p value. These samples are significantly different from each other and show different shell lengths. The small standard error could be due to the overall small standard deviations and large sample size. Standard deviation is directly proportional to standard error and the larger sample size decreases the standard error and makes estimates more precise.

#### 4.3 Calculate meaningful variables from our measured values

Create new columns for:

- territory area in square millimeters from the "`numbsquares`" column

- Limpet body mass from shell length (equation below is from Fenberg et al. 2013).

```{r}
All_Territories_area_mass <- All_Territories |> 
  mutate(area_mm2 = ((19^2) * numbsquares)) |> 
  mutate(mass_g = (0.00009 * size_mm ^ 3.0471)) #mutating columns for area and mass

#total area = 19^2 * number of squares counted 
#mass = formula below

    # create a new column for territory area in mm^2 using the "numbsquares" column
         # mesh = 19 mm x 19 mm 

  # create a new column for limpet body mass
  # formula: mass_g = 0.00009*length ^ 3.0471

```

```{r}
  labs(title = "Treasure Cove Limpet Mass vs. Territory Area", x = "Mass (g)", y = "Territory Area (mm^2)")         #labels :)
```

#### 4.6. What important assumptions of tests of linear regression do these scatter plots fail? How can you tell?

```{r}

# write a linear model for the relationship, then use the plot() function on the model object to show the residuals vs. fitted values and QQ plots to assess your regression. 

view(All_Territories_area_mass)

linear_model <- lm(mass_g ~ area_mm2, data = All_Territories_area_mass )

plot(linear_model)

#The residuals vs fitted plot fails, the data does show not a random amount of variation between points. The points in this graph are extremely clustered on the right end, suggesting a lot of negative residuals, and the fitted red line is not roughly flat. 
#The q-q residuals plot also fails. The points start to strongly curve upwards on the right end of the plot and the overall curved shape fails the normality assumption. The data will need to be transformed for sure. 
```

One way to transform data that has this shape is to apply a log-transformation. Logarithmic relationships are common in biology for mass, volume, or other spatial relationships.

#### 4.7. Plot the relationship between log-transformed mass and log-transformed area. Does this relationship meet assumptions?

```{r scatterplot with regression line}
# plot a scatterplot log area on y axis by log mass_g on x axis, best fit regression line but no SE interval

All_Territories_area_mass |> ggplot() + aes(log(mass_g), log(area_mm2)) + #setting up plot with mass on x, area on y, both log-transformed
  geom_point() +    #point plot :) 
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE) +  #adding regression line, linear model method, no SE zone 
  labs(title = "Limpet Mass vs. Territory Area", x = "log(Mass) (g)", y = "log(Territory area) (mm^2)")  #labels :) 

```

```{r}
# write the linear model object and examine the residual and QQ plots
log_model <- lm(log(area_mm2)~ log(mass_g), data = All_Territories_area_mass) #setting up linear model with both log mass and area, response = area, predictor = mass, data = where to look

plot(log_model, which = 1) #plottin log linear model, 1st plot
plot(log_model, which = 2) #plottin log linear model, 2nd plot

#variance of residuals looks way better, q-q still has little weird ends but overall a lot closer to normal 
```

#### 4.8. What is the formula for the best fit line for the relationship between territory size and body mass in owl limpets?

```{r linear regression test summary}

summary(log_model)  #calling up summary table 

intercept = round(coef(log_model)[1], 4)  #pulling out intercept, 4 decimal points
slope     = round(coef(log_model)[2], 4)  #pulling out slope, 4 decimal points
 
```

**The formula for the best fit line can be extracted from the model summary. The two values in the Estimate column are the coefficients - (Intercept) gives the y-intercept, and the variable gives the slope.**

**log(area) = 0.8903 \* log(mass) + 8.2116**

**or**

**Y = 0.8903 + 8.2116**

Limpet mass and territory size are positively correlated to a significant degree, and there is good evidence that there is a causal relationship between these two variables.
